AMWU FILES FOR PROTECTED INDUSTRIAL ACTION AT BHP PORTS 
While others are telling Pilbara mine workers that BHP's proposed South Flank and Mining Area C Agreement is somehow a step forward, the AMWU is doing what it has always done — fighting hard for mechanical trades workers and organising to build real power.
For months, AMWU members at BHP port operations in Port Hedland have bargained in good faith. They have attended meetings, put forward claims, participated constructively and genuinely tried to reach an agreement that reflects the skills, experience and contribution of the mechanical maintenance workforce.
Other unions in the Pilbara are busy selling workers minimum-rate agreements with no real career progression, weak protections and little certainty for the future. AMWU members at BHP ports are drawing a line in the sand.
The AMWU has now commenced proceedings in the Fair Work Commission seeking a Protected Action Ballot Order.
This is not a step workers take lightly.
Protected industrial action is a lawful right. It exists for a reason. When workers have bargained honestly, reasonably and in good faith, they are entitled to have a meaningful mechanism available to apply pressure when negotiations stall.
Now they are exercising their lawful rights.
The message from Port Hedland maintenance workers is loud and clear:
Enough is enough.
If you're a mechanical tradesperson working for BHP in Port Hedland, South Flank, Mining Area C, Yandi, Jimblebar, Newman, Rail, Ports or anywhere across the Pilbara, now is the time to stand with the union that is actually fighting for mechanical maintenance workers.
Stand and deliver. Join the AMWU.
 United.
 Determined.
 Ready to fight for a fair deal.
#AMWU #PortHedland #Pilbara #UnionStrong #MechanicalTrades #MaintenanceWorkers #ProtectedAction #FairAgreement #BHP

𝐏𝐢𝐥𝐛𝐚𝐫𝐚 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐓𝐨 𝐁𝐞 𝐓𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐬 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝-𝐂𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬
ETU members at BHP  Ports are now voting on whether to endorse protected industrial action in support of their Enterprise Agreement campaign.
Let's be clear about what this vote is about.
Our members are not voting because they want conflict. They are voting because they are determined to ensure that their labour is not valued any less than the labour of their comrades in the South West.
BHP and the paid-for media can spin this however they like, but workers know the reality.
Working in the Pilbara is no longer what it used to be.
The days when employers could expect workers to accept being left behind while company profits soar are over. FIFO life comes with sacrifices. Time away from family comes with sacrifices. Living and working in one of the most remote industrial regions in the country comes with sacrifices.
Workers are simply demanding that those sacrifices are properly recognised and fairly rewarded.
This Protected Action Ballot gives ETU members the opportunity to send a strong message to BHP: enough is enough.
 Every vote matters.
Under Australia's industrial laws, not voting has the same effect as voting NO. If members want a stronger bargaining position and want BHP to understand the strength of feeling across the Ports workforce, they need to participate in the ballot.
The vote is about giving workers a voice and giving workers options. Any future action will be determined by the members themselves.
The message to BHP is simple:
If you want industrial peace, bring a fair offer to the table.
If you want to undervalue Pilbara workers, expect resistance.
Vote. Participate. Stand together.
In Unity,
ETU North West Crew

𝐁𝐇𝐏'𝐒 𝐍𝐔𝐌𝐁𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐃𝐎𝐍'𝐓 𝐀𝐃𝐃 𝐔𝐏
BHP  and their industry lobby group, the The Chamber of Minerals and Energy of Western Australia - CMEWA, an employer union, want workers to believe that asking for a fair Enterprise Agreement is somehow unreasonable.
Let's do the maths.
The media is reporting that industrial action at Port Hedland could put around $𝟏𝟐𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐚𝐲 in exports at risk.
There are approximately 𝟒𝟓𝟎 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬 covered by this agreement.
BHP says workers are already on around $𝟐𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 including allowances and bonuses.
450 workers × $200,000 = $𝟗𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫
Let's be generous and increase that figure.
450 workers × $250,000 = $𝟏𝟏𝟐.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫
Still not there.
450 workers × $280,000 = $𝟏𝟐𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫
Read that again.
𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐰𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 $𝟖𝟎𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬.
Yet BHP would rather threaten disruption, spend millions on lawyers, consultants and anti-union propaganda, and run to the media than sit down and negotiate an agreement that reflects the value workers create.
And what about the outrageous claim being pushed that workers want salaries of $400,000 a year?
Let's test that too.
450 workers × $400,000 = $𝟏𝟖𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫.
Even if that absurd claim were true, it would amount to about 𝟏.𝟒 𝐝𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬.
That's it.
The remaining 𝟑𝟔𝟑.𝟔 𝐝𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬 would still be flowing out of Port Hedland.
So let's stop pretending this dispute is about money.
This is about ideology.
This is about control.
BHP wants workers to remain dependent on management deciding who gets rewarded and who doesn't. They want to continue offering wage outcomes that fail to keep pace with the cost of living while posting massive profits and shipping billions of dollars of Australian resources overseas.
The reality is that ETU members can earn the same money — and often more — in Perth and the South West while sleeping in their own bed every night, watching their kids grow up and being there for life's important moments.
FIFO used to come with a genuine financial advantage.
That advantage has been eroded.
Workers know it.
That's why the Pilbara is unionising.
Workers are realising that the only way to stop falling behind is to stand together, join their union, organise collectively and, when necessary, exercise their lawful right to take protected industrial action.
BHP didn't build the Pilbara.
Workers built the Pilbara.
And workers deserve their fair share.
𝐈𝐟 𝐁𝐇𝐏 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞 $𝟏𝟐𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚 𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦.
 ETU WA
 Organise. Unite. Win.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐁𝐁𝐐 𝐓𝐨 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐞
Workers walked off the job yesterday for the first time in decades at a BHP iron ore operation.
Some sections of the media spent days claiming the sky would fall and that industrial action would cripple production. Then, when the stoppage happened, many of those same voices claimed it had "no impact."
So which is it?
Earlier that day, a car dumper and a ship loader both suffered breakdowns. Union members worked hard to get the equipment back into service until 2:00 pm. Then they downed tools and made history.
The result was simple: ore stayed on the trains, the rail network backed up, stockpiles grew, and ship departures were delayed. It was another reminder of a basic truth that BHP too often forgets:
𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐬.
This first stoppage was just the entrée - a small taste of what is to come if BHP refuses to negotiate a fair Union EBA that protects wages, conditions and secure career progression.
The main course will be far harder for BHP to digest. BHP will need more than some digestives to cure the indigestion.
𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡. 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞.

Yesterday, over 100 Ports Unions members joined the community picket in Port Hedland as part of yesterday's protected industrial action (PIA) where members from WMWA Partner Union the AWU undertook 4 consecutive 1 hour stoppages at the end of day shift and start of night shift, along with members from the ETU and AMWU. 
BHP Ports union members want BHP to take the negotiations for the new Ports agreement seriously, and they don't want to wait 2 years like MAC/South Flank employees had to. 
Taking PIA is never the first option and it's never easy - a big thank you to the Ports Unions members for standing together and standing up yesterday, including all those members who wanted to partake but had to remain at work for safety reasons. 
If you don't fight you lose - WMWA fighting for Fair across the Pilbara!

 A proposed REM models that is fair for all workers at Port Hedland

Earlier this month BHP confirmed a majority of MAC and South Flank employees have voted in support of their new proposed enterprise bargaining agreement.
This week, BHP lodged the proposed agreement to the Fair Work Commission for approval. The approval process normally can take a couple of months and allows for bargaining representatives, including the WMWA partner Unions to raise concerns around things like mandatory content/model clauses and other technical legal issues.
Once approved, the agreement's terms and conditions will apply to the 1800 workers covered by the agreement. It will include:
 4% guaranteed yearly pay increases for all workers.
 Increases to shift allowances for workers not on even time rosters like 8/6 and 8/6-7/7.
 14% super contribution paid from July.
 A higher duties allowance for step up supervisors
 A clearer classification structure (albeit not as detailed or as fair as we wanted)
 An actual clear issue resolution process (albeit not as strong as we wanted)
 A commitment to introduce a delayed compensation flights policy.
The above benefits are the result of hundreds of WMWA members providing BHP with organised and professional feedback on their original baseline proposal, which included only one of the above benefits from the first offer.
WMWA members at MAC and South Flank should be proud of the results they achieved against all the odds.
Meanwhile, the Fight for Fair continues at Port Hedland, with members from WMWA Partner union AWU taking historic protected industrial action yesterday!

AMWU FILES FOR PROTECTED INDUSTRIAL ACTION AT BHP PORTS 
While others are telling Pilbara mine workers that BHP's proposed South Flank and Mining Area C Agreement is somehow a step forward, the AMWU is doing what it has always done — fighting hard for mechanical trades workers and organising to build real power.
For months, AMWU members at BHP port operations in Port Hedland have bargained in good faith. They have attended meetings, put forward claims, participated constructively and genuinely tried to reach an agreement that reflects the skills, experience and contribution of the mechanical maintenance workforce.
Other unions in the Pilbara are busy selling workers minimum-rate agreements with no real career progression, weak protections and little certainty for the future. AMWU members at BHP ports are drawing a line in the sand.
The AMWU has now commenced proceedings in the Fair Work Commission seeking a Protected Action Ballot Order.
This is not a step workers take lightly.
Protected industrial action is a lawful right. It exists for a reason. When workers have bargained honestly, reasonably and in good faith, they are entitled to have a meaningful mechanism available to apply pressure when negotiations stall.
Now they are exercising their lawful rights.
The message from Port Hedland maintenance workers is loud and clear:
Enough is enough.
If you're a mechanical tradesperson working for BHP in Port Hedland, South Flank, Mining Area C, Yandi, Jimblebar, Newman, Rail, Ports or anywhere across the Pilbara, now is the time to stand with the union that is actually fighting for mechanical maintenance workers.
Stand and deliver. Join the AMWU.
 United.
 Determined.
 Ready to fight for a fair deal.
#AMWU #PortHedland #Pilbara #UnionStrong #MechanicalTrades #MaintenanceWorkers #ProtectedAction #FairAgreement #BHP

ETU members at BHP  Ports are now voting on whether to endorse protected industrial action in support of their Enterprise Agreement campaign.
Let's be clear about what this vote is about.
Our members are not voting because they want conflict. They are voting because they are determined to ensure that their labour is not valued any less than the labour of their comrades in the South West.
BHP and the paid-for media can spin this however they like, but workers know the reality.
Working in the Pilbara is no longer what it used to be.
The days when employers could expect workers to accept being left behind while company profits soar are over. FIFO life comes with sacrifices. Time away from family comes with sacrifices. Living and working in one of the most remote industrial regions in the country comes with sacrifices.
Workers are simply demanding that those sacrifices are properly recognised and fairly rewarded.
This Protected Action Ballot gives ETU members the opportunity to send a strong message to BHP: enough is enough.
 Every vote matters.
Under Australia's industrial laws, not voting has the same effect as voting NO. If members want a stronger bargaining position and want BHP to understand the strength of feeling across the Ports workforce, they need to participate in the ballot.
The vote is about giving workers a voice and giving workers options. Any future action will be determined by the members themselves.
The message to BHP is simple:
If you want industrial peace, bring a fair offer to the table.
If you want to undervalue Pilbara workers, expect resistance.
Vote. Participate. Stand together.
In Unity,
ETU North West Crew

BHP  and their industry lobby group, the The Chamber of Minerals and Energy of Western Australia - CMEWA, an employer union, want workers to believe that asking for a fair Enterprise Agreement is somehow unreasonable.
Let's do the maths.
The media is reporting that industrial action at Port Hedland could put around $𝟏𝟐𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐚𝐲 in exports at risk.
There are approximately 𝟒𝟓𝟎 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬 covered by this agreement.
BHP says workers are already on around $𝟐𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 including allowances and bonuses.
450 workers × $200,000 = $𝟗𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫
Let's be generous and increase that figure.
450 workers × $250,000 = $𝟏𝟏𝟐.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫
Still not there.
450 workers × $280,000 = $𝟏𝟐𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫
Read that again.
𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐰𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 $𝟖𝟎𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐥 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬.
Yet BHP would rather threaten disruption, spend millions on lawyers, consultants and anti-union propaganda, and run to the media than sit down and negotiate an agreement that reflects the value workers create.
And what about the outrageous claim being pushed that workers want salaries of $400,000 a year?
Let's test that too.
450 workers × $400,000 = $𝟏𝟖𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫.
Even if that absurd claim were true, it would amount to about 𝟏.𝟒 𝐝𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬.
That's it.
The remaining 𝟑𝟔𝟑.𝟔 𝐝𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬 would still be flowing out of Port Hedland.
So let's stop pretending this dispute is about money.
This is about ideology.
This is about control.
BHP wants workers to remain dependent on management deciding who gets rewarded and who doesn't. They want to continue offering wage outcomes that fail to keep pace with the cost of living while posting massive profits and shipping billions of dollars of Australian resources overseas.
The reality is that ETU members can earn the same money — and often more — in Perth and the South West while sleeping in their own bed every night, watching their kids grow up and being there for life's important moments.
FIFO used to come with a genuine financial advantage.
That advantage has been eroded.
Workers know it.
That's why the Pilbara is unionising.
Workers are realising that the only way to stop falling behind is to stand together, join their union, organise collectively and, when necessary, exercise their lawful right to take protected industrial action.
BHP didn't build the Pilbara.
Workers built the Pilbara.
And workers deserve their fair share.

Workers walked off the job yesterday for the first time in decades at a BHP iron ore operation.
Some sections of the media spent days claiming the sky would fall and that industrial action would cripple production. Then, when the stoppage happened, many of those same voices claimed it had "no impact."
So which is it?
Earlier that day, a car dumper and a ship loader both suffered breakdowns. Union members worked hard to get the equipment back into service until 2:00 pm. Then they downed tools and made history.
The result was simple: ore stayed on the trains, the rail network backed up, stockpiles grew, and ship departures were delayed. It was another reminder of a basic truth that BHP too often forgets:
𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐬.
This first stoppage was just the entrée - a small taste of what is to come if BHP refuses to negotiate a fair Union EBA that protects wages, conditions and secure career progression.
The main course will be far harder for BHP to digest. BHP will need more than some digestives to cure the indigestion.

BHP Ports union members want BHP to take the negotiations for the new Ports agreement seriously, and they don't want to wait 2 years like MAC/South Flank employees had to. 
Taking PIA is never the first option and it's never easy - a big thank you to the Ports Unions members for standing together and standing up yesterday, including all those members who wanted to partake but had to remain at work for safety reasons. 
If you don't fight you lose - WMWA fighting for Fair across the Pilbara!

Earlier this month BHP confirmed a majority of MAC and South Flank employees have voted in support of their new proposed enterprise bargaining agreement.
This week, BHP lodged the proposed agreement to the Fair Work Commission for approval. The approval process normally can take a couple of months and allows for bargaining representatives, including the WMWA partner Unions to raise concerns around things like mandatory content/model clauses and other technical legal issues.
Once approved, the agreement's terms and conditions will apply to the 1800 workers covered by the agreement. It will include:
 4% guaranteed yearly pay increases for all workers.
 Increases to shift allowances for workers not on even time rosters like 8/6 and 8/6-7/7.
 14% super contribution paid from July.
 A higher duties allowance for step up supervisors
 A clearer classification structure (albeit not as detailed or as fair as we wanted)
 An actual clear issue resolution process (albeit not as strong as we wanted)
 A commitment to introduce a delayed compensation flights policy.
The above benefits are the result of hundreds of WMWA members providing BHP with organised and professional feedback on their original baseline proposal, which included only one of the above benefits from the first offer.
WMWA members at MAC and South Flank should be proud of the results they achieved against all the odds.

No actual ‘bargaining’ has occurred in 10 hours of negotiation as INPEX say that they are still trying to “understand our claims”.
INPEX’s have sent OA members correspondence advising that “some of the (union) claims generated more discussion than others…”.

Over 400 Offshore Alliance and AWU members have endorsed the proposed Inpex EA, which sets a new industry standard for wages, conditions and job security across offshore oil and gas!
This new agreement locks in:
• Job Security – Permanent jobs are protected and cannot be outsourced to low-wage labour hire contractors.
• Remuneration – Industry benchmark rates of pay and allowances have been secured.
• Career Progression Framework – A new competency-based progression system will provide clear career pathways and recognition of skills and experience.
• Improved Employee Representation Rights – Enhanced delegates' rights, improved right of entry provisions to offshore facilities, and stronger representation rights for members in disciplinary matters.

Much better rates/salaries that lead the pack, proper level progression, vital job security and minimum manning provisions by classification and facility and more!

This campaign and dispute are a textbook example of how to win against the big end of town. High Union density, organised, capable and unwilling to bend under any circumstance. Congratulations to every INPEX worker involved. You are worth every cent you have secured – and more! Champions! INPEX IR and those in Tokyo – give yourself a whopping uppercut!
Ian Gill

Not once.
This dispute cost INPEX 1 train (which was shut down at ILNG yesterday), 2 Conde tankers and an LNG carrier.

It is a dispute which should have been settled months earlier, had there been a different approach to negotiations.
But the final bargaining outcome is a credit to all parties who have settled their differences and negotiated agreed industrial outcomes.

Had it not been for DP Binet’s efforts in threading the needle through the competing industrial interests, this dispute was headed for a more costly industrial dispute than the 2022 Shell Prelude dispute.
Our Offshore and Onshore INPEX Reps have done a massive job in representing the interests of their workmates and their contribution to bargaining was nothing short of outstanding.
We also want to again thank the efforts of Barrister Oshie Fagir in knocking off the S.424 INPEX application to terminate Protected Industrial Action.
Our INPEX members have now formally named him “King Oshie”
Great work by Offshore Alliance and AWU National Organiser Zach Duncalfe and ETU National Legal Officer Kevin Sneddon who had our members back, every step through the process.
And a big shout out to the efforts of Organizer’s Strawbs, Caleb and Gilly. Great work. And keep those bananas and coke’s going Strawbs! 
As for AREEA and the NT News? They can both go and fXXX themselves.
Offshore Alliance

Over 400 Offshore Alliance and AWU members have endorsed the proposed Inpex EA, which sets a new industry standard for wages, conditions and job security across offshore oil and gas!
This new agreement locks in:
• Job Security – Permanent jobs are protected and cannot be outsourced to low-wage labour hire contractors.
• Remuneration – Industry benchmark rates of pay and allowances have been secured.
• Career Progression Framework – A new competency-based progression system will provide clear career pathways and recognition of skills and experience.
• Improved Employee Representation Rights – Enhanced delegates' rights, improved right of entry provisions to offshore facilities, and stronger representation rights for members in disciplinary matters.
• Improved Overcycle Arrangements – Better roster flexibility and overcycle provisions for offshore workers.
